headline: Tiny African Wildcats Depend on Borrowed Burrows to Raise Young
meta_description: New research reveals Africa's smallest wildcat relies almost entirely on abandoned rodent burrows to shelter and raise kittens in southern Namibia.
summary_short: Scientists tracking black-footed cats in Namibia discovered these endangered felines depend almost entirely on burrows dug by springhares to raise their young safely.
body:
A team of researchers tracking five female black-footed cats across southern Namibia has uncovered a hidden dependency that may be crucial to the survival of Africa's smallest wildcat. Between 2020 and 2021, scientists found that 98% of the underground dens used by these cats to raise their kittens had originally been dug and then abandoned by springhares—small, kangaroo-like rodents endemic to the region. Using laser-based remote-sensing technology to measure tunnel dimensions, researchers determined which species had created each burrow, revealing a striking pattern: the cats consistently selected burrows with entrances between 10 and 27 centimeters in diameter, avoiding both smaller rodent holes and larger aardvark or porcupine tunnels.

With fewer than 10,000 black-footed cats remaining in the wild, understanding their behavior offers rare insight into how these nocturnal hunters survive. Kittens stay sheltered in a single burrow for their first six to seven weeks of life—a critical period when they're most vulnerable. Once the young begin exploring, mothers switch to a new burrow nearly every night, moving through an average of 12 different shelters during the study period. This frequent relocation likely reduces the risk of predation by jackals, caracals, and other threats that hunt young, curious kittens.

The research underscores an often-invisible relationship between species. Though scientists cannot definitively prove black-footed cats would vanish without springhares, the evidence suggests they would become far more vulnerable without access to these ready-made dens. Paradoxically, Africa's most efficient feline hunters—boasting success rates that exceed those of lions or leopards—depend on the survival of a humble rodent for their offspring's safety.
quick_facts: Fewer than 10,000 black-footed cats remain in the wild today
98% of dens studied were abandoned springhare burrows in Namibia
Kittens shelter in one burrow for 6-7 weeks before moving nightly
Mothers used average of 12 different burrows during study period
Black-footed cats are world's most efficient feline hunters
